records.greek: Ταῦτα εἰπὼν Ἰησοῦς ἐξῆλθεν σὺν τοῖς μαθηταῖς αὐτοῦ πέραν τοῦ χειμάρρου τοῦ Κεδρὼν ὅπου ἦν κῆπος, εἰς ὃν εἰσῆλθεν αὐτὸς καὶ οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: These things having said, Jesus went out with the disciples of him across the winter-stream of the Kidron, where was a garden, into which entered he and the disciples of him.

L.1: Having said these things, Jesus went out with His disciples across the winter stream of the Kidron, where there was a garden, into which He and His disciples entered.

R.1: When Jesus had finished praying, He left the city with His disciples and crossed over the Kidron Valley. On the other side there was a garden, and Jesus and His disciples went into it.

decisions.choice: having said these things: after the prayer of chapter 17, Jesus leaves for the place of his arrest
alternatives: after the farewell words of chapters 13-17 as a whole
decisions.reason: "These things" points back to what Jesus has just said, the prayer of chapter 17, which closes the words he spoke to his disciples at the supper (13:31-17:26). In 14:31 he had said, "Rise, let us go from here"; only now does John tell of their going out, from the house where they ate and out of the city.

decisions.choice: the winter stream of the Kidron: the valley east of Jerusalem, whose stream flows only in the rainy season
alternatives: a river that flows all year
decisions.reason: The word χειμάρρου means a stream that runs in winter, when the rains come, and is dry for the rest of the year; it is used of the valley it runs through. The Kidron Valley lies between the eastern wall of Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives. At Passover, in spring, it may have held little water. King David crossed the Kidron when he fled from Jerusalem, betrayed by his counselor (2 Samuel 15:23, 31); John does not draw attention to that.

decisions.choice: a garden: an enclosed plot, probably of olive trees, on the slope of the Mount of Olives
decisions.reason: John says only "a garden". Matthew and Mark name the place Gethsemane (Matthew 26:36; Mark 14:32), a name meaning "oil press", and Luke places it on the Mount of Olives (Luke 22:39). John will also place Jesus's tomb in a garden (19:41).

decisions.choice: of the Kidron, the name of the valley (SBLGNT)
alternatives: of the cedars (many manuscripts, among them some of the oldest)
decisions.reason: The name Kidron sounds like the Greek word for cedar, and many manuscripts, some of them early, read "the winter stream of the cedars". The SBLGNT reads the place name, which is certainly what is meant: the valley is called the Kidron in the Old Testament (2 Samuel 15:23; 1 Kings 15:13). A footnote gives the other reading. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the winter stream of the Kidron (L); the Kidron Valley (B, R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the word for a seasonal stream (meaning decision m2). Balanced and Readable name the valley, which is what a reader can picture and find on a map, since the stream was dry for much of the year.

decisions.choice: had finished praying; left the city; On the other side
alternatives: having said these things; went out (Literal)
decisions.reason: Readable says what "these things" were (the prayer just ended, meaning decision m1) and where Jesus went out from. "On the other side" gives the sense of "across" in a sentence of its own.

records.heading: Jesus is arrested

records.greek: ᾔδει δὲ καὶ Ἰούδας ὁ παραδιδοὺς αὐτὸν τὸν τόπον, ὅτι πολλάκις συνήχθη Ἰησοῦς ἐκεῖ μετὰ τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: Knew now also Judas, the [one] handing over him, the place, because often gathered Jesus there with the disciples of him.

L.2: Now Judas also, the one who was handing Him over, knew the place, because Jesus had often gathered there with His disciples.

R.2: Judas, the one who was betraying Jesus, knew this place too, because Jesus had often met there with His disciples.

decisions.choice: the one handing him over: betraying him, and doing it now
alternatives: the one who would later hand him over
decisions.reason: As in 6:64 and 6:71, the verb means to hand someone over, and for Judas it means betrayal. Here the participle is present: the betrayal is already under way. Judas left the supper to do it (13:27-30).

decisions.choice: had often gathered there: the garden was a regular meeting place
decisions.reason: The adverb means "often", and the verb is the ordinary one for coming together. Luke says Jesus went to the Mount of Olives "as was his custom" (Luke 22:39; compare 21:37). Because it was their habit, Judas knew where to find him at night, away from the crowds.

decisions.choice: handing over (L); betraying (B, R)
decisions.reason: As in 6:64 and 6:71 (rendering decision r-en-1 there): Literal keeps the plain sense of the verb, so that the reader sees it is the word later used of the authorities and of Pilate (18:30, 35; 19:16); Balanced and Readable say what Judas's handing over was (meaning decision m1).

records.greek: ὁ οὖν Ἰούδας λαβὼν τὴν σπεῖραν καὶ ἐκ τῶν ἀρχιερέων καὶ ἐκ τῶν Φαρισαίων ὑπηρέτας ἔρχεται ἐκεῖ μετὰ φανῶν καὶ λαμπάδων καὶ ὅπλων.
records.gloss: So the Judas, having taken the cohort and from the chief priests and from the Pharisees officers, comes there with lanterns and torches and weapons.

L.3: So Judas, having taken the cohort and officers from the chief priests and from the Pharisees, comes there with lanterns and torches and weapons.

R.3: So Judas led a group of Roman soldiers to the garden. Temple guards sent by the leading priests and the Pharisees came with them. They brought lanterns, torches and weapons.

decisions.choice: the cohort: a unit of Roman soldiers from the garrison in Jerusalem; John need not mean the whole unit
alternatives: the temple guard, called by a military word
the whole cohort, several hundred men
decisions.reason: The word σπεῖραν is the usual term for a Roman cohort, at full strength up to about 600 men, and in 18:12 its commander is called by the title of a Roman tribune. Acts uses the same two words for the Roman garrison in Jerusalem, which was on watch at the festivals, when crowds filled the city (Acts 21:31-32). The article may simply name the unit the soldiers came from; a detachment, not all of it, is the likely meaning. John does not say how the Roman soldiers came to be sent; their presence shows that the Roman authorities were involved from the arrest on. The other Gospels speak of a crowd sent by the chief priests (Mark 14:43).

decisions.choice: officers from the chief priests and the Pharisees: the temple police, sent by the council
decisions.reason: These are the officers who kept order in the temple for the chief priests, sent once before to arrest Jesus and come back without him (7:32, 45-46). The chief priests and the Pharisees are the leaders who met in council and gave orders for his arrest (11:47, 57).

decisions.choice: having taken: Judas brought them and guided them to the place
alternatives: Judas was in command of them
decisions.reason: Judas did not command Roman soldiers or the temple police. He took them along as the one who knew the place (verse 2); Acts 1:16 calls him "guide to those who arrested Jesus".

decisions.choice: lanterns, torches and weapons: equipment for a search at night, and for resistance
decisions.reason: A lantern held a small oil lamp shielded from the wind; a torch was a burning brand. Passover fell at the full moon, but they came prepared to search a dark garden among trees, and armed in case Jesus's followers fought.

decisions.choice: comes (L); went, led (B, R); also says (L), asked and said (B, R) in verses 4 and 5
decisions.reason: John often tells past events in the present tense ("he comes", "he says") to make a scene vivid. Literal keeps the present; Balanced and Readable use the past, as stories are normally told. This applies to every such verb in the passage ("comes" in verse 3, "says" in verses 4 and 5).

decisions.choice: the detachment of soldiers, temple police (B); a group of Roman soldiers, temple guards, leading priests (R)
decisions.reason: "Cohort" names a Roman unit that few readers know, so Balanced says "detachment of soldiers" and Readable says plainly whose soldiers they were (meaning decision m1). The officers are named as at 7:32 and 7:45: "temple police" at Balanced, "temple guards" at Readable (meaning decision m2). Readable says "leading priests", as in John 7 and 11, and splits the long sentence.

records.greek: Ἰησοῦς οὖν εἰδὼς πάντα τὰ ἐρχόμενα ἐπ’ αὐτὸν ἐξῆλθεν, καὶ λέγει αὐτοῖς· Τίνα ζητεῖτε;
records.gloss: Jesus therefore, knowing all the things coming upon him, went out, and says to them, "Whom do you seek?"

L.4: So Jesus, knowing all the things that were coming upon Him, went out and says to them, "Whom are you seeking?"

R.4: Jesus knew everything that was going to happen to Him. So He went out to meet them and asked, "Who are you looking for?"

decisions.choice: knowing all that was coming upon him: Jesus goes to meet his arrest knowingly and by his own choice
decisions.reason: John has said that Jesus knew his hour had come (13:1) and knew all that the Father had given into his hands (13:3). He is not caught by surprise: he steps forward himself. He had said that no one takes his life from him, but that he lays it down of his own accord (10:18).

decisions.choice: went out: came out of the garden to meet them
alternatives: stepped forward from among his disciples
decisions.reason: In verse 1 Jesus and his disciples went into the garden; now he goes out toward the men coming for him. The word may also mean only that he stepped forward. Either way he meets them before they find him.

decisions.choice: Whom are you seeking?: Jesus makes them name the one they have come for
decisions.reason: "Seek" runs through John's Gospel. Jesus's first words in it are "What are you seeking?" (1:38), and after the resurrection he asks Mary, "Whom are you seeking?" (20:15). Here those who seek him seek to arrest him, as others had sought to kill him (5:18; 7:1, 30). His question leads them to say his name (verse 5).

decisions.choice: went out to them (B); went out to meet them (R); asked (B, R); Who (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say whom he went out toward (meaning decision m2) and use "asked" for the present "says" before a question (historic present, rendering decision r-en-1 at verse 3). Literal keeps the formal "whom"; Balanced and Readable use everyday "who".

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθησαν αὐτῷ· Ἰησοῦν τὸν Ναζωραῖον.
records.gloss: They answered him, "Jesus the Nazorean."

decisions.choice: the Nazorean: the man from Nazareth
alternatives: a title with a further meaning, such as a play on the "branch" of Isaiah 11:1
decisions.reason: The word Ναζωραῖος is one of two forms used in the New Testament of Jesus as the man from Nazareth; Mark uses the other (Mark 1:24; 14:67), and both mean the same thing (compare Acts 2:22; 22:8). John uses this form only in the arrest and on the notice over the cross (18:5, 7; 19:19). Nazareth was a small town in Galilee, and Jesus was known by it (1:45-46). Matthew links the name with the words of the prophets (Matthew 2:23); John makes no such link. A footnote gives the form of the word.

decisions.choice: the Nazorean (L); of Nazareth (B); from Nazareth (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the form of the word as a title; Balanced and Readable say what it means (meaning decision m1). Balanced and Readable leave out "him" after "answered", which English does not need.

records.greek: λέγει αὐτοῖς· Ἐγώ εἰμι.
records.gloss: He says to them, "I am."

decisions.choice: I am: first of all "I am he", the man you are looking for; the words also echo the way God names himself, which verse 6 brings out
alternatives: the bare "I am", the divine name, as the main sense
only the plain sense, with no echo
decisions.reason: The words have no predicate, but the question supplies one: they are seeking Jesus of Nazareth, and he says he is that man. Verse 8 takes the words up in that sense: "I told you that I am he; so if you are seeking me, let these men go." Yet John repeats the words three times (verses 5, 6 and 8), and when Jesus says them, the men who came to arrest him draw back and fall to the ground (verse 6). "I am" is how God speaks of himself in the Greek of Isaiah (Isaiah 43:10; compare Exodus 3:14), and Jesus has used the words of himself with nothing after them (8:24, 28, 58; 13:19). Here, unlike 8:58, a plain sense fits the words, so it is taken as uppermost, and the echo of God's name is heard within it, as at 6:20. Marked uncertain because the weight between the two senses is a judgment. A footnote gives the bare "I am".

decisions.choice: I am [he] (L); I am he (B, R); also verses 6 and 8
decisions.reason: Because the plain sense is uppermost here (meaning decision m1), every level supplies "he", in brackets at Literal as at 6:20, and it takes the deity_pronoun setting as a pronoun for Christ. "I am he" is also the English used for God's words in Isaiah 43:10 and Deuteronomy 32:39, so the echo can still be heard, which "It is I" or "I am the one" would lose. The same words stand at verses 5, 6 and 8 so the reader sees the repetition. "Said" and "told" stand for the present "says" (rendering decision r-en-1 at verse 3). The footnote gives the bare "I am".

records.greek: εἱστήκει δὲ καὶ Ἰούδας ὁ παραδιδοὺς αὐτὸν μετ’ αὐτῶν.
records.gloss: Had stood now also Judas, the [one] handing over him, with them.

L.5: And Judas also, the one handing Him over, was standing with them.

R.5: Judas, the one who was betraying Jesus, was standing there with them.

decisions.choice: Judas was standing with them: the disciple now stands with those who have come to arrest Jesus
decisions.reason: John places Judas among the arresting party at the moment Jesus names himself. The one Jesus chose as one of the Twelve (6:70-71), who ate bread with him (13:18, 26), now stands on the other side. The verb is pluperfect in form, "had taken his stand", but in this verb that form means simply "was standing".

decisions.choice: the one handing him over: betraying him
decisions.reason: The same present participle as in verse 2 (meaning decision m1 there): the betrayal is happening as John tells it.

decisions.choice: handing over (L); betraying (B, R)
decisions.reason: As in verse 2 (rendering decision r-en-1 there). Readable names Jesus, so that "him" is not taken to mean someone in the arresting party.

records.greek: ὡς οὖν εἶπεν αὐτοῖς· Ἐγώ εἰμι, ἀπῆλθον εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω καὶ ἔπεσαν χαμαί.
records.gloss: When therefore he said to them, "I am," they went away into the [places] behind and fell to-ground.

L.6: So when He said to them, "I am [He]," they went backward and fell to the ground.

R.6: When Jesus said, "I am He," they moved back and fell down on the ground.

decisions.choice: they drew back and fell to the ground: overcome by the one who spoke, they cannot take him until he allows it
alternatives: they stumbled back in surprise or fear, with no further meaning
decisions.reason: John tells it as a direct result of Jesus's words: "when he said ... they drew back and fell". In the Scriptures people fall to the ground before an appearance of God or of his messenger (Ezekiel 1:28; Daniel 10:9; Acts 9:4). The armed men who came to seize Jesus end up on the ground before him; he is arrested only because he gives himself up (10:18; verses 4 and 8).

decisions.choice: possibly the psalms in which the enemies of the righteous are turned back and fall
decisions.reason: Psalm 27:2 says of the psalmist's enemies, "they stumbled and fell", and Psalm 35:4 prays that those who seek his life may be "turned back". John does not quote these psalms, so the echo is uncertain.

decisions.choice: I am: as in verse 5, with the echo of God's name brought out by what follows
decisions.reason: See meaning decision m1 at 18:5. John repeats Jesus's words before telling of the men's fall, which shows that the words themselves, not only the surprise of being met, threw them back.

decisions.choice: I am [he] (L), I am he (B, R); went backward (L), stepped backward (B), moved back (R)
decisions.reason: "I am he" as at verse 5 (rendering decision r-en-1 there). The Greek says they "went away to the things behind", a phrase for moving backward; each level says that in plain words. Balanced and Readable name Jesus as the speaker.

records.greek: πάλιν οὖν ἐπηρώτησεν αὐτούς· Τίνα ζητεῖτε;
records.gloss: Again therefore he asked them, "Whom do you seek?"

L.7: So again He asked them, "Whom are you seeking?"

R.7: Jesus asked them again, "Who are you looking for?"

decisions.choice: he asked them again: Jesus keeps the lead, and makes them name him alone
decisions.reason: The men have fallen to the ground, and it is Jesus, not they, who speaks next. By asking the same question he has them say again that it is Jesus of Nazareth they want, and so he can ask that his disciples go free (verse 8).

decisions.choice: Who is it (B); Who (R)
decisions.reason: As in verse 4 (rendering decision r-en-1 there). Readable names Jesus, since the men have just been the subject.

records.greek: οἱ δὲ εἶπαν· Ἰησοῦν τὸν Ναζωραῖον.
records.gloss: And they said, "Jesus the Nazorean."

decisions.choice: they give the same answer: what happened to them does not change their purpose
decisions.reason: Even after falling to the ground before him, they say the same name. John has noted before that signs did not turn Jesus's opponents from their course (11:47-53; 12:37).

decisions.choice: the Nazorean: the man from Nazareth
decisions.reason: As in verse 5 (meaning decision m1 there).

decisions.choice: of Nazareth (B); from Nazareth (R); answered again (R)
decisions.reason: As in verse 5 (rendering decision r-en-1 there). Readable adds "again" to show that they repeat their first answer (meaning decision m1).

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθη Ἰησοῦς· Εἶπον ὑμῖν ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι· εἰ οὖν ἐμὲ ζητεῖτε, ἄφετε τούτους ὑπάγειν·
records.gloss: Answered Jesus, "I told you that I am; if therefore me you seek, let these to go away";

L.8: Jesus answered, "I told you that I am [He]. So if you are seeking Me, let these [men] go away."

R.8: "I told you that I am He," Jesus answered. "If I am the one you want, let these men go."

decisions.choice: I am: as in verses 5 and 6; here the plain sense is clear from what follows
decisions.reason: See meaning decision m1 at 18:5. "If you are seeking me" shows that "I am" answered their question: he is the Jesus of Nazareth they seek. The third time, after the men have fallen, the words still carry the echo John has drawn out.

decisions.choice: me ... these: Jesus gives himself up so that his disciples go free
decisions.reason: The pronoun "me" is written out and put first for emphasis, set against "these", the disciples. As the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep and does not leave them to the wolf (10:11-12), Jesus hands himself over and asks for his disciples' safety.

decisions.choice: let these go away: a demand, spoken as one in command of the scene
decisions.reason: The verb is an imperative, "allow them to go". Jesus, the one being arrested, tells the arresting party what to do, and the disciples are not taken (verse 9).

decisions.choice: I am [he] (L), I am he (B, R); these [men] (L), these men (B, R); if it is me (B); If I am the one you want (R)
decisions.reason: "I am he" as at verse 5 (rendering decision r-en-1 there). "These" is masculine plural and means the disciples, so "men" is supplied, in brackets at Literal. Balanced and Readable bring out the stress on "me" (meaning decision m2).

records.greek: ἵνα πληρωθῇ ὁ λόγος ὃν εἶπεν ὅτι Οὓς δέδωκάς μοι οὐκ ἀπώλεσα ἐξ αὐτῶν οὐδένα.
records.gloss: So that might be fulfilled the word which he said, "Whom you have given to me, not I lost of them not one."

L.9: [This was] so that the word which He had said might be fulfilled, "Those whom You have given Me, I did not lose one of them."

R.9: This happened so that what Jesus had said would come true: "I have not lost even one of the people You gave Me."

decisions.choice: so that ... might be fulfilled: John's comment on why the disciples went free
decisions.reason: The sentence is the narrator's, not Jesus's. It hangs on verse 8: Jesus asked that his disciples be let go, and they were, so that his own word came true.

decisions.choice: the word he had said: 17:12, and the promise of 6:39 and 10:28
decisions.reason: John quotes freely what Jesus said in his prayer: "I guarded them, and not one of them was lost" (17:12), echoing 6:39, "that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me". "Fulfilled" is the word John uses for Scripture coming true (12:38; 13:18; 17:12; 19:24, 36); here he uses it of Jesus's own word, as again in 18:32.

decisions.choice: I did not lose one: their safety at the arrest is part of Jesus's keeping of them
alternatives: only their physical safety that night
only their eternal safety, with no reference to that night
decisions.reason: In 6:39 and 17:12 not losing them means keeping them for eternal life. John applies the words to their escape from arrest. The two belong together: had the disciples been arrested with him that night, they might not have held out, as Peter's denials show (18:17, 25-27); Jesus keeps them in body so that they are kept for the life he promised.

decisions.choice: [This was] (L); This was so that his own word (B); This happened ... Jesus (R); lose / lost (every level)
alternatives: so that the word might be fulfilled (with no subject)
decisions.reason: English needs a subject for the purpose clause, supplied in brackets at Literal. Readable names Jesus, since the "he" could be misread, and says "come true" for "be fulfilled". Every level uses "lose", as at 6:39 and in the Balanced and Readable text of 17:12, so the reader hears the earlier word. The "you" is the Father and "me" is Jesus, so both take the deity_pronoun setting.

records.greek: Σίμων οὖν Πέτρος ἔχων μάχαιραν εἵλκυσεν αὐτὴν καὶ ἔπαισεν τὸν τοῦ ἀρχιερέως δοῦλον καὶ ἀπέκοψεν αὐτοῦ τὸ ὠτάριον τὸ δεξιόν.
records.gloss: Simon therefore Peter, having a sword, drew it and struck the of the high priest slave and cut off of him the ear the right.

L.10: So Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it and struck the slave of the high priest and cut off his right ear.

R.10: Simon Peter had a sword with him. He pulled it out and swung it at the high priest's servant. It cut off the man's right ear.

decisions.choice: a sword: a short sword or long knife carried for protection
alternatives: a large knife for cutting food
decisions.reason: The word is used of a short sword or a large knife. Men traveling at night might carry one; Luke records that the disciples had two (Luke 22:38). Peter draws it to defend Jesus, against what Jesus has just done in giving himself up (verse 8).

decisions.choice: the high priest's slave: a slave of Caiaphas's household, sent with the arresting party
decisions.reason: The word means a slave, a person owned by another. A high priest's slave might hold a trusted place in his household and act for his master, as this one seems to have done in the arrest. The high priest that year was Caiaphas (verse 13). Another slave of the household, a relative of this man, will recognize Peter (18:26).

decisions.choice: his right ear: all four Gospels tell of it; John alone names Peter and the slave
decisions.reason: Matthew, Mark and Luke each tell that one of those with Jesus cut off the ear of the high priest's slave (Matthew 26:51; Mark 14:47; Luke 22:50). Luke and John say it was the right ear, and Luke adds that Jesus healed it (Luke 22:51). The word for ear is a small form of the usual word, but in the speech of the time it meant simply the ear; it need not mean only the lobe.

decisions.choice: servant
decisions.reason: "Servant" in Balanced and Readable, as the style guide has it; the meaning decision (m2) keeps that the person was owned, and Literal keeps "slave".

decisions.choice: Simon Peter had a sword. He pulled it out ... (B, R); swung it at (R)
alternatives: having a sword, drew it and struck (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable break the participle into short sentences, as English tells an action. Readable says "swung it at" for "struck", since the blow cut off an ear rather than wounding him elsewhere.

records.greek: ἦν δὲ ὄνομα τῷ δούλῳ Μάλχος.
records.gloss: Was now name to the slave Malchus.

L.10: Now the name of the slave was Malchus.

decisions.choice: Malchus: a name used in the region in that period
decisions.reason: The name is found in the region in that period, among Nabateans and others, and is related to the Semitic word for "king". John alone gives it, and he refers to the man again in 18:26, where a relative of his speaks to Peter. Such details suggest that the writer knew the high priest's household (18:15-16).

decisions.choice: the name of the slave was (L); The servant's name was (B, R)
alternatives: There was a name to the slave
decisions.reason: The Greek says "the name to the slave was", a common way of giving a name; English says "his name was".

decisions.choice: servant
decisions.reason: As in the first half of 18:10: "servant" in Balanced and Readable (style guide); Literal keeps "slave".

records.greek: εἶπεν οὖν ὁ Ἰησοῦς τῷ Πέτρῳ· Βάλε τὴν μάχαιραν εἰς τὴν θήκην· τὸ ποτήριον ὃ δέδωκέν μοι ὁ πατὴρ οὐ μὴ πίω αὐτό;
records.gloss: Said therefore the Jesus to the Peter, "Put the sword into the sheath; the cup which has given me the Father, not not shall I drink it?"

L.11: So Jesus said to Peter, "Put the sword into the sheath. The cup which the Father has given Me, shall I not drink it?"

R.11: Jesus told Peter, "Put your sword away! The Father has given Me a cup of suffering to drink, and I will drink it."

decisions.choice: shall I not drink it?: a question that expects "yes, I will"
alternatives: a real question, asking whether he should
decisions.reason: Greek uses two negatives together for the strongest denial; in a question they expect the answer "yes": of course he will drink it. Jesus is not weighing the choice. He has said his soul is troubled, yet he will not ask to be saved from this hour, for he came for it (12:27).

decisions.choice: the cup: the suffering and death the Father has given him; it may also recall the cup of God's judgment
alternatives: only the cup of suffering, with no thought of judgment
the cup of God's judgment as the main sense
decisions.reason: In the Scriptures a cup that God gives to drink can stand for what he appoints for a person, and often for his judgment (Psalm 75:9; Isaiah 51:17, 22; Jeremiah 25:15). In the other Gospels Jesus prays in the garden, "remove this cup from me; yet not what I will, but what you will" (Mark 14:36), and asks his disciples whether they can drink the cup he drinks (Mark 10:38). Here the cup is the suffering and death ahead of him. Whether John also means the cup of judgment, borne for others, he does not say. Marked uncertain on that point.

decisions.choice: the cup the Father has given me: Jesus receives his death from his Father, and Peter's sword stands in the way of it
decisions.reason: Jesus calls God "the Father" and speaks of his death as the Father's gift, using the same verb as in verse 9. Peter would fight to stop the arrest; Jesus will tell Pilate that his servants do not fight, because his kingdom is not from this world (18:36). The order to put the sword away is not only a rebuke but a choice to go the way the Father has given.

decisions.choice: your sword, its sheath (B); Put your sword away (R)
decisions.reason: Greek uses "the" where English says "your" and "its". Readable says simply "away".

decisions.choice: a cup of suffering; and I will drink it (a statement)
alternatives: the cup ... shall I not drink it? (Literal, Balanced)
decisions.reason: Readable says what the cup stands for, keeping to the part that is certain (meaning decision m2), and turns the question into the statement it expects (meaning decision m1).

records.greek: Ἡ οὖν σπεῖρα καὶ ὁ χιλίαρχος καὶ οἱ ὑπηρέται τῶν Ἰουδαίων συνέλαβον τὸν Ἰησοῦν καὶ ἔδησαν αὐτὸν καὶ ἤγαγον πρὸς Ἅνναν πρῶτον· ἦν γὰρ πενθερὸς τοῦ Καϊάφα, ὃς ἦν ἀρχιερεὺς τοῦ ἐνιαυτοῦ ἐκείνου·
records.gloss: The therefore cohort and the commander-of-a-thousand and the officers of the Jews seized the Jesus and bound him, \v 13 and led [him] to Annas first; was for father-in-law of the Caiaphas, who was high priest of the year that;

L.12: So the cohort and the commander and the officers of the Jews seized Jesus and bound Him,
L.13: and they led [Him] to Annas first; for he was father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year.

R.12: Then the Roman soldiers and their commander, together with the temple guards of the Jewish leaders, arrested Jesus. They tied Him up
R.13: and took Him first to Annas. Annas was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was the high priest that year.

decisions.choice: the cohort and the commander: Roman soldiers under their tribune
alternatives: the commander of the temple guard
decisions.reason: The word χιλίαρχος means "commander of a thousand". It was the Greek name for a Roman tribune, the officer over a cohort, and Acts uses it of the tribune of the Roman garrison in Jerusalem (Acts 21:31-33; 22:24). With "the cohort" (meaning decision m1 at verse 3) it shows that Roman soldiers took part in the arrest along with the temple police.

decisions.choice: the officers of the Jews: the temple police of the Jewish authorities
decisions.reason: These are the officers sent by the chief priests and the Pharisees (verse 3; 7:32, 45). "Of the Jews" names the Jewish authorities they served, set beside the Roman soldiers and their commander. It does not mean the Jewish people as a whole: Jesus and his disciples are Jews.

decisions.choice: Annas first: the former high priest, still powerful through his family, questioned Jesus before Caiaphas did
decisions.reason: Annas was high priest from AD 6 to 15, when the Romans removed him. The historian Josephus records that five of his sons held the office after him, and Caiaphas, the high priest in this year, was his son-in-law. Luke and Acts still call him high priest alongside Caiaphas (Luke 3:2; Acts 4:6). "First" looks ahead: after questioning Jesus, Annas sends him to Caiaphas (18:24).

decisions.choice: high priest that year: the year of Jesus's death
alternatives: the office changed hands every year
decisions.reason: As in 11:49 and 11:51 (meaning decision m1 at 11:49): Caiaphas held the office for many years, and "that year" marks the year in which Jesus died.

decisions.choice: seized and bound him: arrested him as a prisoner
decisions.reason: The first verb is the ordinary word for arresting someone; the second is "tie up". Jesus is led away bound, and Annas later sends him to Caiaphas still bound (18:24).

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: Where the word means the authorities, Balanced and Readable name them (see the book's terms and meaning decision m2). The footnote gives the word John wrote.

decisions.choice: the cohort, the commander, the officers (L); the detachment of soldiers, its commander, the temple police (B); the Roman soldiers, their commander, the temple guards (R)
decisions.reason: As in verse 3 (rendering decision r-en-2 there). Every level says "commander", which is what the title meant; "tribune" is the Roman name for the rank (meaning decision m1). Readable breaks the long sentence, ending the first part after "arrested Jesus" so that verse 13 begins at "and took him".

records.greek: ἦν δὲ Καϊάφας ὁ συμβουλεύσας τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις ὅτι συμφέρει ἕνα ἄνθρωπον ἀποθανεῖν ὑπὲρ τοῦ λαοῦ.
records.gloss: Was now Caiaphas the [one] having advised the Jews that it is profitable one man to die for the people.

L.14: Now Caiaphas was the one who had advised the Jews that it is better for one man to die for the people.

R.14: Caiaphas was the one who had told the Jewish leaders it would be best to let one man die for the people.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the members of the council, the chief priests and the Pharisees
decisions.reason: John points back to the meeting of the council in 11:47-53, where Caiaphas spoke to the chief priests and Pharisees gathered there. These are the authorities, not the people as a whole.

decisions.choice: John reminds the reader of Caiaphas's advice in 11:49-52: the man before whom Jesus will stand has already decided that he must die
decisions.reason: The words repeat 11:50 almost exactly, without "for you". Caiaphas meant a political calculation: one man's death to spare the nation. John has said that, as high priest that year, he prophesied without knowing it that Jesus would die for the nation and for the scattered children of God (11:51-52). The outcome of the questioning that follows is already settled.

decisions.choice: it is better ... for the people: to their advantage; on their behalf and in their place
decisions.reason: The verb means "it is profitable" or "it is to someone's advantage", as in 11:50. "For" means on behalf of, and here also instead of (meaning decision m3 at 11:50).

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: Where the word means the authorities, Balanced and Readable name them (see the book's terms and meaning decision m1). The footnote gives the word John wrote.

decisions.choice: it is better (L); it would be better (B); it would be best to let (R); one man ... die for the people (every level)
alternatives: it is to your advantage (as at 11:50)
decisions.reason: Every level keeps "one man" and "die for the people", the words of 11:50, so that the reader hears the echo. Here the Greek has no "for you", so "better" gives the sense of advantage plainly. Balanced and Readable use "would be", as English does in reported advice; Literal keeps the present tense of the original words.

records.greek: Ἠκολούθει δὲ τῷ Ἰησοῦ Σίμων Πέτρος καὶ ἄλλος μαθητής.
records.gloss: Was following now Jesus Simon Peter and another disciple.

L.15: Now Simon Peter was following Jesus, and [so was] another disciple.

R.15: Simon Peter and another disciple followed Jesus.

decisions.choice: another disciple: a follower of Jesus whom John does not name
alternatives: a disciple who was not one of the Twelve
decisions.reason: John does not say who this disciple was. Some have identified him with the disciple whom Jesus loved, because in 20:2-8 that disciple is called "the other disciple", and there too he is paired with Peter, as he is in 13:23-24 and 21:7, 20-21. But here he is "another disciple", not "the other", and nothing in this passage calls him the disciple whom Jesus loved. His acquaintance with the high priest (verse 15b) has led others to think of a disciple from Jerusalem rather than a fisherman from Galilee. The text leaves him unnamed; a footnote mentions the identification with the disciple whom Jesus loved as possible but unproved.

decisions.choice: another disciple, without the article (SBLGNT)
alternatives: the other disciple, with the article (many later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts read "the other disciple", which would point to a disciple the reader already knows, perhaps the one in 20:2. The older manuscripts, among them Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, have no article, and the article looks like an addition that made the identification easier. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: was following: the imperfect pictures them going after Jesus as he was led away
alternatives: followed as his disciples (in the sense of discipleship)
decisions.reason: The verb is the ordinary word for following someone along a road, and the imperfect shows an action going on: they were walking behind the arresting party as it took Jesus to Annas (18:12-13). The word is also John's word for following Jesus as a disciple (1:37-43; 8:12), and Peter had said he would follow Jesus even now (13:36-37); here he does follow, at a distance from the one he follows.

decisions.choice: and [so was] another disciple (L); and so was another disciple (B)
alternatives: Simon Peter and another disciple were following Jesus
decisions.reason: The Greek names Peter first and adds the other disciple at the end, almost as an afterthought; Literal and Balanced keep that order so that Peter stays at the center of the scene. Readable joins the two names as one subject.

records.heading: Peter denies Jesus

records.greek: ὁ δὲ μαθητὴς ἐκεῖνος ἦν γνωστὸς τῷ ἀρχιερεῖ καὶ συνεισῆλθεν τῷ Ἰησοῦ εἰς τὴν αὐλὴν τοῦ ἀρχιερέως, ὁ δὲ Πέτρος εἱστήκει πρὸς τῇ θύρᾳ ἔξω.
records.gloss: That now disciple was known to the high priest and entered with Jesus into the courtyard of the high priest, \v 16 but Peter was standing at the door outside.

L.15: Now that disciple was known to the high priest, and he entered with Jesus into the courtyard of the high priest,
L.16: but Peter was standing at the door outside.

R.15: The high priest knew that disciple, so he went into the high priest's courtyard with Jesus.
R.16: But Peter stood outside at the door.

decisions.choice: known to the high priest: acquainted with him, perhaps closely
alternatives: known only by sight to the household
decisions.reason: The word means someone known to another, an acquaintance; it can be used of relatives and friends (Luke 2:44; 23:49). It was enough for the disciple to be let in himself and to have Peter let in at his word (verse 16). John does not say how the acquaintance came about.

decisions.choice: the courtyard: the open court inside the high priest's house, entered by a door from the street
decisions.reason: A large house was built around an open courtyard, closed to the street by a wall with a door kept by a doorkeeper (Acts 12:13-14). Those who were let in stood in the courtyard, and from there one could see into the rooms around it. John does not say whether Annas and Caiaphas lived in the same house; Jesus was brought to Annas first (18:13) and later sent to Caiaphas (18:24).

decisions.choice: but Peter was standing outside: a contrast with the disciple who went in
decisions.reason: The sentence sets the two disciples side by side: one goes in with Jesus, the other is left standing outside the door. The tense of "was standing" pictures Peter waiting there until the other disciple came for him.

decisions.choice: The high priest knew that disciple, so he went ...
alternatives: That disciple was known to the high priest, and he went ...
decisions.reason: Readable turns the sentence round so that it has an active verb, and says "so" because being known to the high priest is what let him in, as verse 16 shows.

records.greek: ἐξῆλθεν οὖν ὁ μαθητὴς ὁ ἄλλος ὁ γνωστὸς τοῦ ἀρχιερέως καὶ εἶπεν τῇ θυρωρῷ καὶ εἰσήγαγεν τὸν Πέτρον.
records.gloss: Went out therefore the disciple the other the [one] known of the high priest and spoke to the doorkeeper and brought in Peter.
pieces: to the woman who kept the door

L.16: So the other disciple, the one known to the high priest, went out and spoke to the doorkeeper and brought Peter in.

R.16: So the other disciple, the one the high priest knew, came back out. He spoke to the young woman who was watching the door, and then he brought Peter inside.

decisions.choice: brought Peter in: the other disciple is the one who brings him in
decisions.reason: The verb does not show who its subject is, and the doorkeeper has just been mentioned. But the other disciple is the subject of the two verbs before it (went out, spoke), and the sentence reads most naturally with him as the subject of all three. Either way, Peter is let in because of the other disciple.

decisions.choice: the doorkeeper: a woman whose task was to keep the door of the house
decisions.reason: The article with the word is feminine, and verse 17 says that the doorkeeper was a slave girl. Women kept the door of a house in other stories too (Acts 12:13; 2 Samuel 4:6 in the Greek version).

decisions.choice: the woman who kept the door (B); the young woman who was watching the door (R)
decisions.reason: "Doorkeeper" does not show that this was a woman, which the Greek article does (meaning decision m2). Balanced and Readable say so here, so that the servant girl in verse 17 is clearly the same person.

records.greek: λέγει οὖν τῷ Πέτρῳ ἡ παιδίσκη ἡ θυρωρός· Μὴ καὶ σὺ ἐκ τῶν μαθητῶν εἶ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τούτου;
records.gloss: Says therefore to Peter the slave girl the doorkeeper, Not also you of the disciples are of the man this?

L.17: So the slave girl, the doorkeeper, says to Peter, "You are not also [one] of the disciples of this man, are you?"

R.17: The servant girl at the door said to Peter, "You are not one of this man's disciples too, are you?"

decisions.choice: slave girl: a young female slave of the household
decisions.reason: The word is the feminine of the word for a young slave and was the usual word for a female slave, often a young one (Acts 12:13; 16:16; Galatians 4:22-23). She belonged to the high priest's household, as did the male slaves in verses 18 and 26. She is one of the lowest people in the house, and it is her question that Peter cannot answer truthfully.

decisions.choice: a question that expects the answer no
decisions.reason: The word that opens the question shows that the speaker expects a denial: "You are not ..., are you?" The question leaves Peter an easy way out, and he takes it. The same form returns in verse 25.

decisions.choice: also: you too, as well as the other disciple, or as well as others who follow him
decisions.reason: "Also" may mean that the doorkeeper knew the other disciple to be a follower of Jesus, since he had just spoken with her and brought Peter in; or it may simply mean "you as well as the man's other followers". The text does not settle it.

decisions.choice: this man: Jesus, named without his name
decisions.reason: The doorkeeper speaks of Jesus as "this man", the prisoner who has just been brought in. The phrase can carry contempt (9:16, 24), but here it need be no more than a way of pointing to the man under arrest.

decisions.choice: says (L); said (B, R); also verse 26
decisions.reason: John often tells past events in the present tense ("says") to make a scene vivid. Literal keeps the present; Balanced and Readable use the past, as stories are normally told. This applies to every such verb in the passage ("says" twice in verse 17 and once in verse 26).

decisions.choice: servant girl
decisions.reason: "Servant girl" in Balanced and Readable, as the style guide has it for a female slave; the meaning decision (m1) keeps that she was owned, and Literal keeps "slave girl".

records.greek: λέγει ἐκεῖνος· Οὐκ εἰμί.
records.gloss: Says that one, Not I am.

decisions.choice: I am not: Peter's words stand in contrast with Jesus's "I am" in the garden
alternatives: an ordinary denial with no further meaning
decisions.reason: A few verses earlier Jesus answered those who came to arrest him with "I am" (18:5, 6, 8), giving himself up so that his disciples could go free (18:8-9). Now Peter, asked whether he belongs to Jesus, says the same two words with a "not": "I am not." John tells the two scenes one after the other, and the contrast is plain on the page. Whether John meant it as a deliberate echo cannot be proved, since "I am not" is also the ordinary way to say "no" to such a question. John the Baptist used the same words truthfully when he denied that he was the Christ (1:20-21).

decisions.choice: that one: Peter
decisions.reason: The pronoun points back to Peter, to whom the question was put. It is the first of the three denials Jesus foretold (13:38).

decisions.choice: "No, I am not," Peter said.
decisions.reason: Readable names Peter and adds "No" to make the answer sound natural, and keeps "I am not" so that the words match those in verse 25.

records.greek: εἱστήκεισαν δὲ οἱ δοῦλοι καὶ οἱ ὑπηρέται ἀνθρακιὰν πεποιηκότες, ὅτι ψῦχος ἦν, καὶ ἐθερμαίνοντο· ἦν δὲ καὶ ὁ Πέτρος μετ’ αὐτῶν ἑστὼς καὶ θερμαινόμενος.
records.gloss: Were standing now the slaves and the officers, a charcoal fire having made, because cold it was, and they were warming themselves; was now also Peter with them standing and warming himself.

L.18: Now the slaves and the officers were standing [there], having made a charcoal fire, because it was cold, and they were warming themselves; and Peter also was with them, standing and warming himself.

R.18: It was cold, so the servants and the temple guards had made a charcoal fire. They stood around it to keep warm. Peter stood there with them, warming himself too.

decisions.choice: slaves: the high priest's household slaves
decisions.reason: These are slaves of the high priest's household, like Malchus (18:10) and his relative (verse 26), and the slave girl at the door (verse 17). A wealthy household such as the high priest's had many slaves, who served in the house and on its business; their master owned them, and they had no freedom of their own.

decisions.choice: the officers: the temple police who had made the arrest
decisions.reason: These are the officers of the chief priests who came with Judas and arrested Jesus (18:3, 12), the men who kept order in the temple for the priests (7:32, 45-46). The Roman soldiers who had also been there (18:3, 12) are not mentioned here.

decisions.choice: a charcoal fire, because it was cold: a fire of glowing coals on a cold spring night
decisions.reason: The word means a heap of burning charcoal, which gives heat and a little light. Passover falls in early spring, and Jerusalem stands high in the hills, so the nights can be cold. The fire draws Peter into the circle of the men who had arrested Jesus.

decisions.choice: a charcoal fire: the same word as in 21:9, where the risen Jesus restores Peter
alternatives: no connection between the two scenes
decisions.reason: This word is used only twice in the New Testament: here, where Peter denies Jesus three times, and in 21:9, where the risen Jesus has a charcoal fire burning by the lake before he asks Peter three times whether he loves him (21:15-17). John may mean the reader to remember this fire there. The link rests on one word, so it cannot be proved.

decisions.choice: temple police (B); temple guards (R)
decisions.reason: As in 7:32 and 7:45, Balanced and Readable say whose officers these were (meaning decision m2). The household slaves are "servants" in Balanced and Readable (style guide), kept apart from the temple police or guards.

decisions.choice: had made a charcoal fire ... standing around it (B); It was cold, so ... (R)
alternatives: were standing, having made a charcoal fire (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced puts the making of the fire first, since it came first, and says they stood "around it", which the Greek implies. Readable gives the reason first, in its own sentence.

decisions.choice: servants
decisions.reason: "Servant" in Balanced and Readable, as the style guide has it; the meaning decision (m1) keeps that the person was owned, and Literal keeps "slave".

records.greek: Ὁ οὖν ἀρχιερεὺς ἠρώτησεν τὸν Ἰησοῦν περὶ τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ καὶ περὶ τῆς διδαχῆς αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: The therefore high priest questioned Jesus concerning the disciples of him and concerning the teaching of him.

L.19: So the high priest questioned Jesus about His disciples and about His teaching.

R.19: Meanwhile the high priest asked Jesus questions about His disciples and about what He taught.

decisions.choice: the high priest: Annas, who is questioning Jesus before he sends him to Caiaphas
alternatives: Caiaphas, the high priest of that year (18:13)
decisions.reason: Jesus was taken "first" to Annas (18:13), and only after this questioning did Annas send him to Caiaphas (verse 24), so the questioner here is most naturally Annas. Annas had been high priest some years before (about AD 6 to 15) and was the father-in-law of Caiaphas (18:13). Former high priests kept the title, and Annas remained powerful: five of his sons became high priest. Luke too calls him high priest alongside Caiaphas (Luke 3:2; Acts 4:6). Others read "the high priest" here as Caiaphas, who is called that in 18:13 and 24; a footnote gives that view.

decisions.choice: So: John returns from the courtyard to Jesus
decisions.reason: The word picks up the story of Jesus where it left off in 18:13-14, while Peter is in the courtyard. John moves between the two scenes, Peter's denials (verses 15-18 and 25-27) and Jesus's questioning (verses 19-24), so that the reader sees both at once: Jesus stands firm while Peter gives way.

decisions.choice: about his disciples and his teaching: who his followers were and what he taught them
decisions.reason: The questions seem meant to find grounds for a charge: how large his following was, and whether his teaching led people astray (7:12, 47). Jesus answers about his teaching and says nothing about his disciples, the ones he had protected at his arrest (18:8-9).

decisions.choice: Meanwhile
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "Meanwhile" to show that the scene changes while Peter stands by the fire (meaning decision m2).

records.heading: Jesus before the high priest

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθη αὐτῷ Ἰησοῦς· Ἐγὼ παρρησίᾳ λελάληκα τῷ κόσμῳ· ἐγὼ πάντοτε ἐδίδαξα ἐν συναγωγῇ καὶ ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ, ὅπου πάντες οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι συνέρχονται, καὶ ἐν κρυπτῷ ἐλάλησα οὐδέν·
records.gloss: Answered him Jesus, I openly have spoken to the world; I always taught in synagogue and in the temple, where all the Jews come together, and in secret I spoke nothing;

L.20: Jesus answered him, "I have spoken openly to the world; I always taught in synagogue and in the temple, where all the Jews come together, and in secret I spoke nothing.

R.20: Jesus answered, "I have spoken openly to the world. I have always taught people in synagogues and in the temple courts, where all the Jews meet together. I have not said anything in secret.

decisions.choice: openly: in public, where anyone could hear
decisions.reason: The word means openness in speech, and here, set against "in secret" at the end of the verse, it means in public. It is the word used when Jesus taught openly in the temple (7:26) and when he stopped going about openly (11:54). In 10:24 and 16:25, 29 it means plain speech instead; that is not the sense here.

decisions.choice: the world: people at large, anyone who would listen
alternatives: the world as opposed to God (15:18)
decisions.reason: Here the world is simply everyone: Jesus did not teach a closed circle but spoke where all could hear (compare 7:4, where his brothers told him to show himself to the world).

decisions.choice: the Jews: the Jewish people, who gathered in the synagogues and the temple
decisions.reason: Here the word means the Jewish people as a whole, who came together for worship and teaching in their synagogues and, at the festivals, in the temple in Jerusalem. Jesus taught them all in the open (6:59; 7:14, 28; 10:23). It does not mean the authorities, so every level keeps "the Jews".

decisions.choice: in synagogue: in synagogues, wherever he taught
decisions.reason: The word has no article, which gives a general sense: in synagogue gatherings, such as the one at Capernaum (6:59). The temple has the article, because there was only one.

decisions.choice: I said nothing in secret: possibly an echo of God's words in Isaiah
alternatives: no allusion; a plain statement of fact
decisions.reason: In Isaiah 45:19 and 48:16 God says that he has not spoken in secret. Jesus's words may echo these, but they are also a plain answer to a hearing held at night, away from the crowds: what he taught was never hidden.

decisions.choice: synagogues; temple courts
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use the plural for the general sense of the word without an article (meaning decision m4), and say "temple courts" for the whole temple area, as John's word means (see docs/john-terms.md).

records.greek: τί με ἐρωτᾷς;
records.gloss: Why me do you question?

R.21: Why are you asking Me these questions?

decisions.choice: why question me: a case was to be proved by witnesses
alternatives: a refusal to answer anything at all
decisions.reason: In the law of Moses a charge had to be established by the evidence of witnesses (Deuteronomy 17:6; 19:15), and Jesus himself speaks of the need for witnesses (8:17). He asks why he is being questioned when there are witnesses to hand, and points to them in the next sentence. He does not refuse to speak; he asks for a fair hearing.

decisions.choice: asking me these questions
decisions.reason: Readable says "these questions" so that the plain verb "ask" keeps the sense of questioning.

records.greek: ἐρώτησον τοὺς ἀκηκοότας τί ἐλάλησα αὐτοῖς· ἴδε οὗτοι οἴδασιν ἃ εἶπον ἐγώ.
records.gloss: Question those having heard what I spoke to them; behold, these know what said I.

L.21: Question those who have heard what I spoke to them; look, these know what I said."

R.21: Ask the people who heard Me teach. They know what I said."

decisions.choice: look, these know: the people who heard him know what he said
alternatives: Jesus points to particular people present in the room
decisions.reason: "These" refers back to "those who have heard". The word "look" may mean that Jesus pointed to people standing there, perhaps the officers who once came back saying that no one had ever spoken like him (7:46); but it may simply draw attention to what he says. The text does not say that he pointed.

decisions.choice: those who have heard: the people who listened to his public teaching
decisions.reason: These are the many who heard him teach in the open (verse 20). The perfect tense stresses that they are still there to be asked.

decisions.choice: the people who heard me teach
alternatives: those who heard what I said to them
decisions.reason: Readable says "teach" to tie the sentence to verse 20, and leaves out "look", which a reader might take to mean that Jesus pointed.

records.greek: ταῦτα δὲ αὐτοῦ εἰπόντος εἷς παρεστηκὼς τῶν ὑπηρετῶν ἔδωκεν ῥάπισμα τῷ Ἰησοῦ εἰπών· Οὕτως ἀποκρίνῃ τῷ ἀρχιερεῖ;
records.gloss: These things now of him having said, one standing by of the officers gave a slap to Jesus, having said, Thus you answer the high priest?

L.22: Now when He had said these things, one of the officers standing by gave Jesus a slap, saying, "Is this how You answer the high priest?"

R.22: When Jesus said this, one of the temple guards standing there slapped Him. "Is that any way to answer the high priest?" he said.

decisions.choice: gave a slap: a blow with the open hand, an insult as much as an injury
alternatives: a blow with a rod or club
decisions.reason: The word first meant a blow with a stick, but by this time it was commonly used of a slap with the open hand, usually in the face. A slap was a public insult. The same word is used in Mark 14:65 and in 19:3, and in the Greek version of Isaiah 50:6, where the servant of the Lord gives his cheeks to blows. A blow with a rod cannot be ruled out; a footnote gives it.

decisions.choice: Is this how you answer: a rebuke for a lack of respect
alternatives: a real question about the content of the answer
decisions.reason: The officer treats Jesus's words as insolence toward the high priest. The law commanded respect for a ruler of the people (Exodus 22:28, quoted by Paul in a similar scene, Acts 23:2-5).

decisions.choice: the officers: the temple police
decisions.reason: The same men as in verse 18, who served the chief priests (7:32; 18:3, 12).

decisions.choice: temple police (B); temple guards (R); slapped (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the officers as in verse 18. "Slapped" says what kind of blow it most likely was (meaning decision m1).

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθη αὐτῷ Ἰησοῦς· Εἰ κακῶς ἐλάλησα, μαρτύρησον περὶ τοῦ κακοῦ· εἰ δὲ καλῶς, τί με δέρεις;
records.gloss: Answered him Jesus, If wrongly I spoke, testify concerning the wrong; if however rightly, why me do you strike?

L.23: Jesus answered him, "If I spoke wrongly, testify concerning the wrong; but if rightly, why do you strike Me?"

R.23: Jesus answered, "If I said something wrong, then be a witness and show everyone what was wrong. But if what I said was right, why do you hit Me?"

decisions.choice: testify concerning the wrong: give evidence of what was wrong
decisions.reason: The verb is John's word for bearing witness (1:7; 5:31-39; 8:14-18), and here it has its legal sense: if the answer broke the law, let the officer act as a witness and prove it. Jesus asks again for evidence instead of blows (verse 21).

decisions.choice: if wrongly ... if rightly: two possibilities set side by side
decisions.reason: The two conditions do not mean that Jesus is unsure; they put the officer to the test. If he cannot show any wrong, the blow was unjust. "Wrongly" and "rightly" are the common words for badly and well.

decisions.choice: strike: beat or hit
decisions.reason: The verb means to beat or hit someone. Jesus speaks of the blow just given (verse 22); the present tense makes the question vivid: why are you striking me?

decisions.choice: be a witness and show everyone what was wrong
decisions.reason: Readable explains "testify" by what a witness does (meaning decision m1); "everyone" makes plain that testimony is given before others.

records.greek: ἀπέστειλεν οὖν αὐτὸν ὁ Ἅννας δεδεμένον πρὸς Καϊάφαν τὸν ἀρχιερέα.
records.gloss: Sent therefore him Annas bound to Caiaphas the high priest.

L.24: So Annas sent Him bound to Caiaphas the high priest.

R.24: Then Annas sent Jesus to Caiaphas the high priest. Jesus was still tied up.

decisions.choice: So Annas sent him: the next step in the story, after the questioning
alternatives: Annas had sent him, so that verses 19-23 took place before Caiaphas
decisions.reason: "So" moves the story on: when the questioning got nowhere, Annas sent Jesus to Caiaphas. Some have read the verb as "had sent", so that the questioning in verses 19-23 took place before Caiaphas; but the Greek tense is the ordinary past for the next event, and the word "so" fits a step forward. Some manuscripts read "and" or have no connecting word, and one early Syriac translation rearranges these verses; the SBLGNT reading is followed. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: Annas and Caiaphas: the former high priest and the high priest in office
decisions.reason: Annas was Caiaphas's father-in-law (18:13). Caiaphas was the high priest in office that year (11:49; 18:13), and it was he who had advised that one man should die for the people (18:14). John does not tell what happened before Caiaphas; the next scene is in the morning at Pilate's headquarters (18:28).

decisions.choice: bound: still tied as he had been since the arrest
decisions.reason: Jesus was tied up when he was arrested (18:12). The perfect tense shows that he stayed bound; Annas, though he found no charge, did not set him free.

decisions.choice: still bound (B); Jesus ... still tied up (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "still" to show that he had been bound since the arrest (meaning decision m3). Readable names Jesus and puts his being tied up in a sentence of its own.

records.greek: Ἦν δὲ Σίμων Πέτρος ἑστὼς καὶ θερμαινόμενος.
records.gloss: Was now Simon Peter standing and warming himself.

L.25: Now Simon Peter was standing and warming himself.

R.25: All this time Simon Peter was still standing by the fire, warming himself.

decisions.choice: Simon Peter was standing: the story returns to Peter in the courtyard
decisions.reason: The words repeat the end of verse 18 almost exactly. John takes the reader back to the courtyard, where Peter has been all the time that Jesus was being questioned.

decisions.choice: Meanwhile ... still standing there (B); All this time ... still standing by the fire (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "still" and "Meanwhile" or "All this time" so that the reader sees that the scene has gone back to Peter by the fire of verse 18 (meaning decision m1).

records.heading: Peter denies him again

records.greek: εἶπον οὖν αὐτῷ· Μὴ καὶ σὺ ἐκ τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ εἶ;
records.gloss: They said therefore to him, Not also you of the disciples of him are?

L.25: So they said to him, "You are not also [one] of His disciples, are you?"

R.25: So the men there said to him, "You are not one of His disciples too, are you?"

decisions.choice: they said: the men standing at the fire
decisions.reason: The verb is plural and has no stated subject, so it means the slaves and officers standing with Peter by the fire (verse 18). The other Gospels tell this second question differently (Matthew 26:71; Mark 14:69; Luke 22:58); John says only that several of those present asked it.

decisions.choice: a question that expects the answer no
decisions.reason: The question has the same form as the doorkeeper's (verse 17): "You are not ..., are you?" Again it leaves Peter an easy way to deny.

decisions.choice: the men there
decisions.reason: Readable says who "they" were (meaning decision m1).

records.greek: ἠρνήσατο ἐκεῖνος καὶ εἶπεν· Οὐκ εἰμί.
records.gloss: Denied that one and said, Not I am.

L.25: He denied [it] and said, "I am not."

R.25: Peter denied it. "I am not," he said.

decisions.choice: denied: disowned Jesus by saying he did not belong to him
decisions.reason: This is the verb Jesus used when he foretold that Peter would deny him three times (13:38). Peter denies not a belief but his own tie to Jesus: "I am not" one of his disciples. John the Baptist is said to have "confessed and not denied" (1:20); Peter does the reverse.

decisions.choice: I am not: the second time Peter says it
decisions.reason: Peter repeats his words of verse 17 (see meaning decision m1 there on the contrast with Jesus's "I am").

decisions.choice: denied [it] (L); denied it (B, R)
decisions.reason: The Greek verb has no object; English needs "it", which Literal brackets. "Deny" is kept at every level, as in 13:38 at Literal and Balanced, so that the reader sees Jesus's words coming true.

records.greek: λέγει εἷς ἐκ τῶν δούλων τοῦ ἀρχιερέως, συγγενὴς ὢν οὗ ἀπέκοψεν Πέτρος τὸ ὠτίον· Οὐκ ἐγώ σε εἶδον ἐν τῷ κήπῳ μετ’ αὐτοῦ;
records.gloss: Says one of the slaves of the high priest, a relative being of [him] whose cut off Peter the ear, Not I you saw in the garden with him?

L.26: One of the slaves of the high priest, being a relative of [the one] whose ear Peter cut off, says, "Did I not see you in the garden with Him?"

R.26: One of the high priest's servants was a relative of Malchus, the man whose ear Peter had cut off. He said to Peter, "I saw you in the garden with Him, did I not?"

decisions.choice: a relative of the man whose ear Peter cut off: a kinsman of Malchus
decisions.reason: Peter had cut off the right ear of the high priest's slave Malchus when Jesus was arrested (18:10). This man, a slave of the same household, was a relative of Malchus and had evidently been there in the garden. Of the three who question Peter, he has the most reason to recognize him, and the most reason to be hostile.

decisions.choice: Did I not see you: a question that expects the answer yes, with stress on "I"
alternatives: a question that expects no, like those in verses 17 and 25
decisions.reason: Unlike the first two questions, this one is framed to expect agreement, and the man says "I" with emphasis: I saw you myself. The first two questions gave Peter a way out; this one is a challenge from an eyewitness.

decisions.choice: the garden: the place across the Kidron valley where Jesus was arrested
decisions.reason: John has told that Jesus went with his disciples across the Kidron to a garden, a place where he often met with them (18:1-2), and that he was arrested there.

decisions.choice: Malchus
alternatives: the man whose ear Peter had cut off
decisions.reason: Readable gives the name of the slave, which John has already told the reader (18:10), so that the link is easy to follow; it also puts the question in a form that clearly expects yes (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: servants
decisions.reason: "Servant" in Balanced and Readable (style guide); Literal keeps "slave".

records.greek: πάλιν οὖν ἠρνήσατο Πέτρος· καὶ εὐθέως ἀλέκτωρ ἐφώνησεν.
records.gloss: Again therefore denied Peter, and immediately a rooster crowed.

L.27: So again Peter denied [it], and immediately a rooster crowed.

R.27: Once more Peter denied it. Right then a rooster crowed.

decisions.choice: the third denial and the rooster: what Jesus foretold has come true
decisions.reason: Jesus had said that a rooster would not crow until Peter had denied him three times (13:38). Now the third denial is made and the rooster crows at once. John does not say what Peter did next; the other Gospels say that he remembered Jesus's words and wept (Matthew 26:75; Mark 14:72; Luke 22:61-62). In John, Peter's story is taken up again after the resurrection (20:2-10; 21:15-19).

decisions.choice: a rooster crowed: the crowing of a bird, in the hours before dawn
alternatives: the Roman trumpet signal at the end of the third watch of the night, called cockcrow
decisions.reason: Roosters crow in the small hours before dawn, and that part of the night could be called "cockcrow" (Mark 13:35). Some have suggested that the trumpet call that marked that watch is meant, but the plain sense is the bird, as Jesus's words in 13:38 suggest. The next scene begins "early" (18:28).

decisions.choice: at that moment (B); Right then (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say that the rooster crowed just as Peter finished speaking, which is what "immediately" means here.

records.greek: Ἄγουσιν οὖν τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἀπὸ τοῦ Καϊάφα εἰς τὸ πραιτώριον· ἦν δὲ πρωΐ· καὶ αὐτοὶ οὐκ εἰσῆλθον εἰς τὸ πραιτώριον, ἵνα μὴ μιανθῶσιν ἀλλὰ φάγωσιν τὸ πάσχα.
records.gloss: They lead therefore the Jesus from the Caiaphas into the praetorium; it was now early; and they not entered into the praetorium, that not they might be defiled but might eat the Passover.

L.28: So they lead Jesus from Caiaphas into the praetorium. Now it was early. And they themselves did not enter into the praetorium, so that they might not be defiled, but might eat the Passover.

R.28: Then they took Jesus from Caiaphas to the palace of the Roman governor. It was very early in the morning. The men who had brought Him did not go inside the palace. They wanted to stay ritually clean so that they could eat the Passover meal.

decisions.choice: the praetorium: the headquarters of the Roman governor
decisions.reason: The word is a Latin military term taken into Greek. It was first a general's tent, then the residence and headquarters of a Roman governor (Matthew 27:27; Acts 23:35). The governor of Judea normally lived at Caesarea on the coast and came up to Jerusalem at the great festivals. Whether his Jerusalem headquarters was the former palace of Herod the Great or the Antonia fortress beside the temple is not known for certain.

decisions.choice: early: the last part of the night, around dawn
decisions.reason: The word names the last of the four watches of the night, after the rooster crows (Mark 13:35); the rooster had just crowed (18:27). Jesus is brought to the governor at first light.

decisions.choice: defiled: made ritually unclean by entering a Gentile's dwelling
decisions.reason: The defilement is ritual, not moral. Jews held that going into the house of a Gentile made a person unclean (Acts 10:28; 11:3); later Jewish teaching, collected in the Mishnah, counts the dwellings of Gentiles as unclean (Oholot 18:7). A person who was unclean could not eat the Passover at its proper time (Numbers 9:6-13). John sets their care over ritual purity beside their pressing for an innocent man's death.

decisions.choice: eat the Passover: the Passover meal, still ahead on the day of the trial
alternatives: the festival offerings eaten during the following days of the feast
decisions.reason: In John the Passover meal has not yet been eaten when Jesus is tried and crucified: the day is "the day of Preparation of the Passover" (19:14), and the Sabbath that follows is "a great day" (19:31). In Matthew, Mark and Luke, the meal Jesus ate with his disciples the night before was a Passover meal (Mark 14:12-16; Luke 22:15). The phrase can also mean the festival meals eaten during the seven days of the feast (compare 2 Chronicles 30:21-22), and on that reading the accounts agree in their timing. How they fit together is not settled here; the plain sense of John is followed.

decisions.choice: they: those who held Jesus at Caiaphas's house, the chief priests and their officers
alternatives: the Jewish people as a whole
decisions.reason: The verb has no named subject; it carries on from 18:24-27. Pilate later says that the chief priests handed Jesus over (18:35), and the chief priests and their officers are the ones who shout for his crucifixion (19:6). "They themselves" sets these men, who stay outside, against Jesus, who is taken in.

decisions.choice: Historic present: they lead, says (L); led, said (B, R)
decisions.reason: John often tells past events in the present tense to make them vivid ("they lead", "he says"). Literal keeps the present throughout this passage so that readers see the Greek form; Balanced and Readable use the past, the normal tense for telling a story in English. This decision covers every historic present in 18:28-40 (also "says" in 18:29 and 18:38).

decisions.choice: the governor's headquarters (B); the palace of the Roman governor (R)
decisions.reason: "Praetorium" is a Latin word few readers know, so Balanced and Readable say what the building was (meaning decision m1). Readable names the governor as Roman, since the story turns on the difference between the Jewish authorities and the Roman court. Verse 33 uses the same words.

decisions.choice: to avoid becoming ritually unclean (B); the men who had brought him, stay ritually clean, the Passover meal (R)
alternatives: so that they would not be defiled
decisions.reason: "Defiled" could be taken as moral corruption, so Balanced and Readable say it was a matter of ritual cleanness (meaning decision m3). Readable names the subject as the men who had brought Jesus, without saying more than the text (meaning decision m5), and says "meal" for the Passover (meaning decision m4).

records.heading: Jesus before Pilate

records.greek: ἐξῆλθεν οὖν ὁ Πιλᾶτος ἔξω πρὸς αὐτοὺς καὶ φησίν· Τίνα κατηγορίαν φέρετε κατὰ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τούτου;
records.gloss: Went out therefore the Pilate outside to them and says, "What accusation do you bring against the man this?"

L.29: So Pilate went out to them and says, "What accusation do you bring against this man?"

R.29: So Pilate came out to meet them. "What do you accuse this man of?" he asked.

decisions.choice: Pilate: Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor of Judea
decisions.reason: Pilate governed Judea for Rome from about AD 26 to 36 (Luke 3:1). A stone inscription found at Caesarea in 1961 calls him "prefect of Judea". John brings him into the story without introduction, as a figure his readers knew. Only the governor could order an execution (18:31).

decisions.choice: went out ... outside: the scene moves between the courtyard outside and the headquarters inside
decisions.reason: Because the accusers will not come in (18:28), Pilate goes back and forth: out to them here, in to Jesus (18:33), out again (18:38), in (19:9), out (19:4, 13). The doubled "went out outside" marks the first move. The questioning of Jesus happens inside; the shouting happens outside.

decisions.choice: accusation: a formal charge brought before a judge
decisions.reason: The word is a legal one. Pilate opens a hearing in proper form by asking for the charge.

decisions.choice: What charge are you making (B); What do you accuse this man of (R)
decisions.reason: Plain modern words for the legal question (meaning decision m3). The historic present "says" is covered by decision r-en-1 at 18:28.

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθησαν καὶ εἶπαν αὐτῷ· Εἰ μὴ ἦν οὗτος κακὸν ποιῶν, οὐκ ἄν σοι παρεδώκαμεν αὐτόν.
records.gloss: They answered and said to him, "If not was this [man] evil doing, not [would] to you we have handed over him."

L.30: They answered and said to him, "If this [man] were not doing evil, we would not have handed Him over to you."

R.30: "He is a criminal," they answered. "If He were not, we would not have handed Him over to you."

decisions.choice: were not doing evil: a man who habitually does wrong, a wrongdoer
decisions.reason: The verb "to be" with the participle "doing" describes an ongoing practice. They name no crime. Pilate asked for a charge (18:29); they answer that their own handing over should be proof enough.

decisions.choice: handed over: the word used again and again for Jesus's betrayal and surrender
decisions.reason: The same verb is used of Judas (18:2, 5), of the chief priests (18:35), of what Jesus' servants would have prevented (18:36), and of Pilate himself (19:16). It traces the chain by which Jesus is passed from hand to hand to the cross.

decisions.choice: handed over, at every level
decisions.reason: One English phrase is kept for this verb through the passion story so that readers can follow the chain (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: We would not have handed him over to you if this man were not a wrongdoer (B); He is a criminal ... If he were not (R)
alternatives: If this man were not doing evil (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced puts the main clause first and uses a noun for the ongoing practice (meaning decision m1). Readable states the claim first in a short sentence; it says no more than "doing evil" implies.

records.greek: εἶπεν οὖν αὐτοῖς ὁ Πιλᾶτος· Λάβετε αὐτὸν ὑμεῖς, καὶ κατὰ τὸν νόμον ὑμῶν κρίνατε αὐτόν.
records.gloss: Said therefore to them the Pilate, "Take him you, and according to the law of you judge him."

L.31: So Pilate said to them, "You take Him, and judge Him according to your law."

R.31: Pilate said to them, "Take Him away and put Him on trial yourselves, by your own law."

decisions.choice: you take him: the stressed "you" pushes the case back to them
decisions.reason: "You" is added in Greek where it is not needed, which stresses it. Since they have named no crime against Roman law, Pilate tells them to deal with the man themselves.

decisions.choice: your law: the Law of Moses, applied in the Jewish courts
decisions.reason: Rome let the peoples it ruled settle many matters by their own laws and courts. In Judea the high priest and the council judged cases under the Law of Moses. Pilate treats the matter as an internal religious dispute.

decisions.choice: judge: try in court and give a verdict
decisions.reason: The verb has its legal sense here, as in 7:51 ("Does our law judge a man without first hearing him?").

decisions.choice: try (B); put on trial (R)
decisions.reason: In modern English "judge" can mean simply to form an opinion of someone; "try" makes the court setting plain (meaning decision m3).

records.greek: εἶπον αὐτῷ οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι· Ἡμῖν οὐκ ἔξεστιν ἀποκτεῖναι οὐδένα·
records.gloss: Said to him the Jews, "For us not it is lawful to kill anyone";

L.31: The Jews said to him, "It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death."

R.31: But the Jewish leaders answered, "We are not allowed to put anyone to death."

decisions.choice: the Jews: the chief priests and their officers who brought Jesus to Pilate
alternatives: the Jewish people as a whole
decisions.reason: They are the ones who led Jesus from Caiaphas (18:28) and who, Pilate says, handed him over (18:35); at 19:6 the chief priests and their officers shout for his death. The word names this group of leaders, not the people: Jesus and his disciples are Jews, and so are many who believed in him (11:45; 12:11).

decisions.choice: not lawful for us: under Roman rule only the governor could order a man's death
alternatives: it was not lawful to execute anyone during the festival
it was not lawful for them to crucify
decisions.reason: When Rome took direct rule of Judea in AD 6, Josephus says the first governor was sent with power over life and death (Jewish War 2.117). Some events seem to go against this: the stoning of Stephen (Acts 7:58), and the execution of James the Lord's brother in AD 62 while there was no governor in the province, for which the high priest was removed from office (Josephus, Antiquities 20.200-203). So the rule may have had exceptions, or such killings may have been unlawful. John's point is plain either way: they need Pilate to sentence Jesus.

decisions.choice: the answer shows that they want a death sentence, not a trial
decisions.reason: Pilate offered them a trial under their own law; their reply shows that they have already decided on death. "For us" is put first for stress: they cannot do it, Pilate can. The purpose clause of verse 32 hangs on this exchange.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: Where the word means the authorities, Balanced and Readable name them (see the book's terms). The footnote gives the word John wrote.

decisions.choice: not permitted to execute (B); not allowed to put to death (R)
decisions.reason: "Kill" here means a lawful execution after a sentence, not murder (meaning decision m2).

records.greek: ἵνα ὁ λόγος τοῦ Ἰησοῦ πληρωθῇ ὃν εἶπεν σημαίνων ποίῳ θανάτῳ ἤμελλεν ἀποθνῄσκειν.
records.gloss: that the word of the Jesus might be fulfilled which he said signifying by what kind of death he was about to die.

L.32: [This was] so that the word of Jesus might be fulfilled which He spoke, signifying by what kind of death He was about to die.

R.32: This happened so that what Jesus had said would come true. He had pointed to the kind of death He was going to die: He would be lifted up on a cross.

decisions.choice: the word of Jesus: his saying about being lifted up (12:32-33; compare 3:14; 8:28)
alternatives: a saying about being handed over to the Gentiles (Mark 10:33)
decisions.reason: The words "signifying by what kind of death he was about to die" repeat 12:33 exactly, where John explained Jesus's saying "when I am lifted up from the earth". Death by Jewish sentence would have been by stoning (8:59; 10:31); because Jesus is handed to the Roman governor, he will die by the Roman penalty of crucifixion, raised up on a cross.

decisions.choice: so that ... might be fulfilled: what happens carries out what Jesus foretold
decisions.reason: John uses this language for Scripture being fulfilled (12:38; 13:18; 19:24, 36), and here, as at 18:9, for Jesus's own words. The authorities' refusal to try Jesus themselves leads, beyond their intent, to the death he had already named.

decisions.choice: signifying: indicating by a hint, not saying outright
decisions.reason: The verb means to point to something by a sign. Jesus had spoken in a picture ("lifted up"), not in plain words, as at 12:33 and 21:19.

decisions.choice: [This was] (L); This was (B); This happened (R); he would be lifted up on a cross (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek purpose clause hangs on the exchange in verse 31; English needs a main clause, so every level supplies one, Literal in brackets. Readable also says what kind of death was meant, as at 12:33 (meaning decision m1). The narrator, not a character, gives the explanation.

records.greek: Εἰσῆλθεν οὖν πάλιν εἰς τὸ πραιτώριον ὁ Πιλᾶτος καὶ ἐφώνησεν τὸν Ἰησοῦν καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Σὺ εἶ ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων;
records.gloss: Entered therefore again into the praetorium the Pilate and called the Jesus and said to him, "You are the king of the Jews?"

L.33: So Pilate entered again into the praetorium and called Jesus and said to Him, "Are You the King of the Jews?"
